claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by simultaneous, rapid, and uniform conversion of the metal precursors.
Simultaneous, rapid, and uniform precursor conversion forces the constituent metals to nucleate nearly concurrently.
Synchronized nucleation minimizes local differences in reduction kinetics.
Synchronized nucleation prevents thermodynamically driven phase separation or elemental segregation.
Delayed or nonuniform precursor conversion causes preferential nucleation of one or more metals.
Preferential nucleation promotes phase separation and uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed starting mixture is molecularly or colloidally homogenized and has near-equal precursor ratios.
A single-step, rapid, spatially uniform energy input is intended to induce synchronous precursor conversion.
Rapid, uniform energy input minimizes transient local concentration gradients by shortening the period in which differential reduction kinetics can operate.
During early nucleation, atomic diffusion is insufficient to produce elemental segregation under the proposed rapid-conversion conditions.
Uniform and rapid energy delivery generates all constituent metal atoms nearly simultaneously from their precursors.
Nearly simultaneous metal-atom generation kinetically traps the elements in a mixed configuration before longer-range diffusion can cause phase separation.
Differences in precursor reduction kinetics cause sequential nucleation when nucleation is not simultaneous.
Rapid, homogeneous energy input will produce nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution and a high degree of alloying.
Rapid, homogeneous energy input will produce controlled and reproducible nanoparticle morphology.
The resulting morphology will preserve a high surface-area-to-volume ratio favorable for catalysis.
A slower or spatially nonuniform baseline will show phase segregation, elemental islands, or heterogeneous morphology.
The proposed mechanism should apply when noble-metal precursors have relatively comparable reduction potentials and solubilities and when precursor-conversion and nucleation timescales overlap.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when precursor chemistries differ extremely or when reducing or capping agents independently dominate the kinetics.
